name: Crystallised cane sugar in north India
summary: People in north India boiled cane juice into solid sugar that could be stored and traded; a text said to date from 300 BCE or earlier lists rock sugar.
description: Boiling cane juice and precipitating the impurities gives a moist brown sugar, and further refining gives purer grades. According to Sahapedia, a north Indian document of 300 BCE or earlier already distinguished five kinds of sugar, including khanda or rock sugar; the document is not named and its date could not be checked.

impact.note: Solid cane sugar spread from the Subcontinent to Persia, the Islamic world, the Mediterranean and beyond until most of humanity ate it; it was a new storable foodstuff around which trade and plantation agriculture were organised, and a whole refining industry grew from it. Scored from general knowledge of the spread, of which the source read supports only the westward part.

date.label: by 300 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: According to Sahapedia, a north Indian document of 300 BCE or earlier already mentions five kinds of sugar, including khanda, a rock sugar. The document is not named.

evidence.supports: By 300 BCE, a north Indian document already mentions five kinds of sugar including a type called khanda or rock sugar
evidence.locator: Section on the history of sugar in India

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The source does not name the north Indian document or cite a reference for it. If it is the Arthashastra, its date is disputed and may be several centuries later than 300 BCE, which would explain the lead's wider window of 300 BCE to 350 CE. A scholarly source (Galloway 1989, or Daniels in Science and Civilisation in China) should replace this event's dating.
The same page says South Asian references to sarkara, granular sugar, begin by about 500 BCE; no text is named, so it is not an event here.
The 647 CE Chinese mission for sugar-making know-how is not verified and is not an event here.
The coordinates are an approximate centre of the Ganges plain; no site is known.

research.note: Sahapedia places the earliest references to granular and rock sugar in South Asia and describes sugar cane and then refining spreading west from the Subcontinent to Persia and the Mediterranean afterwards; no earlier solid sugar elsewhere is reported.
